cret-114.title: Zealandia drifts off and the Tasman Sea opens
cret-114.text: The sea between Australia and New Zealand was born when a continent broke away. Zealandia, stretching from New Caledonia to New Zealand's subantarctic islands, separated from Australia about 85 million years ago. About 83 million years ago, a rift entering eastern Tasmania split the Lord Howe Rise from the South Tasman Rise. The Lord Howe Rise, a ribbon of continental crust 3,000 km long, drifted away. Rifting opened the Tasman Sea, and new ocean crust formed in the deep Tasman Basin. Together with {{ref:cret-090}}, this left Zealandia an isolated, mostly drowned continent.

cret-113.title: The High Arctic volcanoes flare again
cret-113.text: Some volcanic provinces erupt for tens of millions of years. The High Arctic Large Igneous Province was active from about 130 to 60 million years ago. About 85 million years ago it entered a second phase. From then until about 60 million years ago, it poured out mildly alkaline flood basalts, a chemically distinct lava from its earlier eruptions.

cret-115.title: The magnetic field's long calm ends
cret-115.text: For 37 million years, Earth's compass never flipped. That long stretch without polarity reversals is called the Cretaceous Normal Superchron, or C34n. A polarity reversal is the moment when magnetic north and south swap places. Calibrated ages place the superchron from 120.964 million years ago to the start of chron C33r at 83.650 million years ago. When it ended, the field began reversing again. Since then, reversals have generally become slowly more frequent.

cret-117.title: India breaks free and races north
cret-117.text: India began the fastest continental journey in this course about 83 million years ago. It rifted from Madagascar and drifted rapidly north toward Eurasia. The Indian plate's run, covering about 6,000 km, began around 84 million years ago. By the Paleocene it was moving about 18 cm a year. By about 83.5 million years ago, new seafloor was spreading between India and Antarctica, unevenly near the Kerguelen Plateau. Madagascar was left behind, flooded with Late Cretaceous basalts up to 200 m thick. India's long trip would end in a collision that raised the Himalayas.

cret-118.title: The North Atlantic begins to open
cret-118.text: The Atlantic opened from south to north, and by the Late Cretaceous the crack was reaching the far north. The ocean began opening between Ireland and Greenland after 85 million years ago. By about 83 million years ago, seafloor spreading had begun between the Rockall Basin and North America. Seafloor spreading is the creation of new ocean crust as two plates move apart. Rifting among the Eurasian, Greenland and North American plates may have started around 81 million years ago, the first steps in splitting the northern continents.

cret-116.title: Iberia turns and pushes into Europe
cret-116.text: The Pyrenees owe their existence to Spain's slow shove against France. The Bay of Biscay finished opening into ocean by about 84 million years ago. From about 83 million years ago, Iberia converged with Europe, until it stopped moving relative to Europe 67.7 million years ago. In the Pyrenees, squeezing had already replaced stretching by the early Turonian, about 90 million years ago.

cret-119.title: The Ninety East Ridge, a 5,000 km volcanic trail
cret-119.text: A single straight ridge runs 5,000 km across the floor of the Indian Ocean. The Kerguelen hotspot built this Ninety East Ridge between 82 and 38 million years ago. A hotspot is a fixed plume of hot mantle that punches volcanoes through the plate above it. This one sat at or near a spreading ridge, and as {{ref:cret-117}} carried India north, it left a long line of volcanic rock behind.

cret-120.title: The oldest Hawaiian–Emperor volcanoes
cret-120.text: The Hawaiian Islands are only the youngest end of a chain of volcanoes. Its oldest dated volcano, at the far northern end, is 81 million years old. The Emperor seamounts, the oldest and most eroded part of the chain, are 39 to 85 million years old. Each formed over the same hotspot and was then carried away by the moving Pacific plate.

cret-121.title: The first palm trees
cret-121.text: Palms, the emblem of tropical beaches, have roots deep in the age of dinosaurs. The first palm trees appear around 80 million years ago. They joined a world already being transformed by flowering plants, and their later spread became a useful sign of warm climates.

cret-123.title: Zeleny Gai, a small Ukrainian crater
cret-123.text: Not every impact can be pinned down precisely. A small one made the Zeleny Gai crater in Ukraine, 3.5 km across. Its age is known only loosely: 80 ± 20 million years ago, a window wide enough to straddle much of the Late Cretaceous.

cret-122.title: The Laramide orogeny raises the Rockies
cret-122.text: The Rocky Mountains began rising far inland, a long way from any plate edge. Mountain building began in western North America in the Late Cretaceous, 80 to 70 million years ago. It unfolded as buoyant terranes, slabs of crust too light to sink, were scraped onto the continent during subduction of the Farallon plate. This Laramide orogeny raised the Rockies. It also started uplifting the Grand Canyon region around 75 million years ago.

cret-124.title: Lappajärvi, a Finnish lake in an impact crater
cret-124.text: One of Finland's largest lakes fills a hole punched by an asteroid. A rock about 1.6 km across struck about 77.85 million years ago, in the Campanian. It left a crater about 22–23 km wide and 750 m deep. Today that crater holds Lake Lappajärvi.

cret-125.title: Dinosaur Park, Alberta's riverside graveyard
cret-125.text: Few places on Earth hold as many dinosaurs as a stretch of Alberta badlands. Rivers draining to {{ref:cret-089}} laid down the Dinosaur Park Formation about 76.5–74.8 million years ago, burying many skeletons with their bones still joined. Dinosaur Provincial Park is one of the world's richest dinosaur sites, with 58 dinosaur species among nearly 500 species of fossil life. Such coastal plains, and their diverse communities, were later lost as the seas retreated.

cret-128.title: The first Velociraptor
cret-128.text: The real Velociraptor was a feathered hunter of the Late Cretaceous. It first appears around 75 million years ago. It became one of the most famous of the small predatory dinosaurs, and one was later found locked in combat in {{ref:cret-127}}.

cret-127.title: The Fighting Dinosaurs of the Gobi
cret-127.text: Two dinosaurs died mid-fight and stayed that way for millions of years. In Mongolia's Djadokhta Formation, a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops were buried locked in combat 75–71 million years ago. The pair gives direct evidence of predatory or aggressive behavior among non-avian dinosaurs. How they were buried so suddenly is debated. Suggestions include drowning, a collapsing dune and a sandstorm.

cret-129.title: The Manson impact in Iowa
cret-129.text: Beneath the cornfields of Iowa lies a buried scar from space. An asteroid or comet nucleus struck near present-day Manson about 74 million years ago. It left an impact structure about 35 km across, now hidden under younger sediment.

cret-130.title: The Atlantic floods Patagonia
cret-130.text: At the end of the Cretaceous, the Atlantic reached all the way to the foot of the young Andes. Foreland basins east of the mountains were sinking, and in the Maastrichtian, Atlantic waters flooded in to reach the mountain front. This transgression, an advance of the sea over land, laid down the marine Jagüel and Roca formations in Patagonia. The flooding lasted from the Maastrichtian into the Danian.

cret-131.title: The last Bennettitales
cret-131.text: Bennettitales looked a little like cycads, and for a long time they were everywhere. These seed plants, also called cycadeoids, had been around since the Permian and were widespread in the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous. Then flowering plants rose, and Bennettitales declined severely through the Late Cretaceous. They died out in most areas toward the end of the period. Their last northern records come from polar latitudes.

cret-133.title: The Maastrichtian sea-level fall
cret-133.text: In the final stage of the Cretaceous, the seas drained off the continents faster than at any other time in the Mesozoic. Sea level fell further during this Maastrichtian regression than in any other Mesozoic interval. A regression is a retreat of the sea from the land, exposing old seafloor and shrinking shallow coastal habitats. The drop came just before the end of the dinosaurs, and it is one of the proposed contributors to {{ref:cret-148}}.

cret-136.title: The Maastrichtian chill
cret-136.text: The last few million years of the Cretaceous were a time of surprising cold. About 70.5 million years ago, surface and bottom waters cooled sharply, and marine species richness rose by 43%. Cooling peaked about 67.5 million years ago, with surface waters at 13 °C, and richness and productivity began to fall. The Western Interior Seaway was coldest early in the Maastrichtian, about 16 °C, before warming to about 22 °C. From the mid-Maastrichtian, more carbon was stored in the deep sea, possibly through cooling and stronger deep circulation. Near the very end, ice sheets and sea ice appear to have briefly returned to Antarctica.

cret-138.title: Mosasaurus, the last giant sea lizard
cret-138.text: The mosasaur that gave the whole group its name arrived late. Mosasaurus evolved around 70 million years ago. By the Maastrichtian, several large mosasaurs shared the Tethys Sea and competed for its prey. They were the ruling marine predators right up to the end of the Cretaceous.

cret-139.title: Multituberculates, rodents before rodents
cret-139.text: Long before mice and squirrels existed, another group of mammals filled their roles. Multituberculates increased in diversity around 70 million years ago. In the Late Cretaceous they radiated as plant-eaters and into forms like squirrel-like tree dwellers, reaching a peak of diversity. They were among the most successful mammals of the age of dinosaurs.

cret-140.title: The Labrador Sea begins to open
cret-140.text: Greenland began drifting away from North America near the end of the Cretaceous. The Labrador Sea started opening 69 million years ago, in the Maastrichtian. Seafloor spreading in its southern part pushed Greenland north relative to North America. The date is not settled: a 1989 paper dates the sea's first opening to 92 million years ago, not 69.

cret-141.title: Modern birds before the asteroid
cret-141.text: Ducks and their relatives were already flying when the dinosaurs died. Vegavis, from the Maastrichtian, shows that modern birds had begun diversifying before the Cenozoic. Asteriornis, also Maastrichtian, appears close to Galloanserae, the fowl group that was the earliest branch of the neognaths. A Vegavis specimen dated 69–66 million years ago holds the oldest known syrinx, the voice organ of birds.

cret-143.title: Quetzalcoatlus, a giant of the skies
cret-143.text: One of the largest animals ever to fly appeared just before the end of the Cretaceous. Quetzalcoatlus, a giant pterosaur, first appears around 68 million years ago. It was among the very last flying reptiles, and its line would end with {{ref:cret-152}}.

cret-144.title: Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops arrive
cret-144.text: The most famous dinosaur matchup in history happened only at the very end. Tyrannosaurus, the largest land predator of western North America, appears in the fossil record 68–66 million years ago. The first species of Triceratops shows up at the same time. Armored Ankylosaurus lived then too and was among the last non-avian dinosaurs. These giants are latecomers: they had only about two million years before the asteroid of {{ref:cret-147}} ended their world.

cret-142.title: Hell Creek, the last dinosaur world
cret-142.text: Montana's Hell Creek Formation is where the dinosaurs' final chapter is written. Its rocks record rivers, deltas and swamps on the low eastern coast facing {{ref:cret-089}}. It yields Tyrannosaurus and Ankylosaurus, and it is a key record of dinosaurs right up to the K–Pg boundary. This Lancian fauna is closer to East Asian and Canadian–Alaskan faunas than most earlier North American ones.

cret-145.title: The Deccan Traps flood India with lava
cret-145.text: India holds about 1.5 million cubic kilometers of lava from a single episode of eruptions. The Deccan Traps began erupting in western India 66.25 million years ago, fed largely by the Réunion hotspot. Most of the lava poured out between 66 and 65 million years ago. It came in three phases, two before the K–Pg boundary and one after. The eruptions warmed climate about 3 °C over the last 100,000 years of the Cretaceous, with a brief 5 °C cold snap 30,000 years before the boundary. Plant fossils record a 250 ppm rise in carbon dioxide across the boundary, likely from Deccan activity. Once proposed as a major extinction cause, the Traps are now generally held to have played a minor role at most. That view is contested, though, and some sources still favor a joint cause.

cret-147.title: The Chicxulub asteroid strikes
cret-147.text: In a single moment, a rock about 10 km wide ended the age of dinosaurs. The asteroid struck just off the Yucatán Peninsula and left the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across. Megatsunamis swept the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. Debris fell across the whole planet as a clay rich in iridium, a metal rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The clay also holds shocked quartz, grains crushed by enormous pressure, and tektites, droplets of melted glass. Then came an impact winter. Dust and soot lingered, sunlight faded, photosynthesis halted, and the oceans rapidly acidified. Argon dating in 2013 gave an age of 66.043 ± 0.043 million years, matching the K–Pg boundary, and impact glass matches the boundary ash. Chicxulub is widely accepted as the primary cause of {{ref:cret-148}}. It is the only mass extinction definitively tied to an impact.

cret-148.title: The Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction
cret-148.text: About three-quarters of all species on Earth disappeared in what may have been a geological instant. The K–Pg extinction wiped out about 76% of species and 47% of genera, including all non-avian dinosaurs. It was the fifth and latest of the great mass extinctions. On land, every animal heavier than 25 kg died, along with all pterosaurs and many mammals, birds, lizards, insects and plants. At sea it killed plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, ammonites and rudist clams. Over 90% of coccolithophore species, the chalk-making plankton, vanished, and about 60% of reef-coral genera. The killing was fast, perhaps under 10,000 years. Ocean productivity and circulation then collapsed for at least tens of thousands of years. Yet some survived. All major mammal lineages and most turtles came through. Mammals then spread into the large-animal niches that the dinosaurs left empty, a story picked up in {{ref:pale-007}}.

cret-149.title: The last ammonites
cret-149.text: Ammonoids, the coiled-shell cousins of squid, had survived for about 410 million years. They vanished during or soon after the K–Pg extinction. Their tiny drifting eggs and larvae were devastated in the upheaval. Of all the cephalopods, only nautiloids and coleoids, the line of squid and octopus, made it through. A few ammonite genera, such as Baculites and Hoploscaphites, may have lingered briefly into the earliest Danian.

cret-150.title: The last belemnites
cret-150.text: Belemnites, squid-like animals with bullet-shaped internal shells, were already in trouble before the asteroid hit. By then they had shrunk to a few high-latitude regions. The K–Pg extinction finished them. As with ammonites, their embryos probably could not survive the acidifying ocean. Sea butterflies, small swimming snails, took the place of their larvae in the food chain.

cret-152.title: The last pterosaurs
cret-152.text: The first vertebrates to fly under their own power did not survive the asteroid. Azhdarchid and nyctosaurid pterosaurs were still present in the Maastrichtian, and likely died out at the K–Pg boundary. In the end every pterosaur perished in that extinction. The skies passed entirely to the birds.

cret-153.title: A New Jersey bone bed from the day of disaster
cret-153.text: Very few fossil sites capture the K–Pg mass death itself. One is a bone bed in New Jersey's Hornerstown Formation, called the Main Fossiliferous Layer. The 66-million-year-old layer is packed with marine life from the shallow sea that once covered southern New Jersey. Iridium and shocked quartz in the layer suggest it formed as ecosystems collapsed during the extinction.

cret-154.title: The end of the non-avian dinosaurs
cret-154.text: Look in Maastrichtian rocks on any continent and dinosaurs are there; look in the rocks just above and they are gone. Scientists agree that all non-avian dinosaurs, then an estimated 628 to 1,078 species, died out at the K–Pg boundary. Birds are the only dinosaur lineage left. Their large size may have left them exposed, along with few small species and no known ability to burrow, swim or dive. Whether they were already declining is uncertain. Dates published in 2025 on New Mexico beds show diverse faunas into the latest Maastrichtian. Titanosaurs, the last long-necked sauropods, were still thriving when the extinction struck.

cret-155.title: Shiva, a disputed second crater
cret-155.text: Some researchers think Chicxulub may not have struck alone. Sankar Chatterjee and colleagues proposed that a structure off India, the potential Shiva crater, formed at the K–Pg boundary and helped cause the extinction. At 450–600 km across, it would far exceed Chicxulub, and it has been dated to about 66 million years ago. But Shiva is only a proposed impact structure, and it has not been confirmed.

cret-156.title: Rudist reefs and giant inoceramids vanish
cret-156.text: Some Cretaceous reefs were built not by corals but by clams. These reef-building rudists died out at the K–Pg boundary, along with the giant inoceramid bivalves. Rudists were once thought to have vanished half a million years early, but they apparently fell to the K–Pg event itself. Inoceramids, known from the Permian to the latest Cretaceous, included true giants. Inoceramus shells exceeded 1 m, and one Greenland specimen reached 1.87 m. Most inoceramids, though, had been declining long before the end.

cret-157.title: Tanis, a snapshot of the impact's first hour
cret-157.text: Within minutes of the impact, 3,000 km away, the ground in North Dakota began to shake. At Tanis, seismic waves raised seiche waves, sloshing surges in an enclosed sea, 10–100 m high in {{ref:cret-089}}. The waves flung marine, freshwater and land animals and plants inland. At the same time, microtektites, tiny glass beads blasted from Yucatán, rained down from the sky. Fossil fish from the site even suggest the impact struck in the Northern Hemisphere spring.

reviews.late-cretaceous-epoch: The Late Cretaceous was a hothouse world that slowly cooled, then ended in a single violent moment. Seas rose high enough to split North America and Africa, while marine reptiles, mosasaurs and giant pterosaurs ruled sea and sky. Continents kept breaking apart: Zealandia, India and the North Atlantic all began their drift. Then the Chicxulub asteroid struck, and about 76% of species vanished, among them every non-avian dinosaur, pterosaur and ammonite. Birds, crocodilians and mammals, all lineages that had appeared during the epoch, came through to inherit the world.

cret-115.text: A swap of Earth's magnetic north and south poles.

cret-119.text: A long-lived plume of hot mantle that builds volcanoes on the plate passing over it.

cret-147.text: A metal rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, found concentrated in the K–Pg boundary clay.
A droplet of natural glass formed from rock melted and thrown out by an impact.

cret-130.text: An advance of the sea over land as sea level rises or land sinks.
